transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. [Your Name]. Can I start by asking your name, and what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. I'm Susan. Susan Abernathy. And, gosh, as for what brings me in... well, it's a bit of a long story, but I guess the main thing is that I just feel so wound up almost all day long. It's this physical feeling, like my whole body is constantly bracing for something, even when there's absolutely no reason for it. 

I work on a computer all day—I've been in database management since I got my bachelor's degree, so I'm very used to desk work and staring at screens. You'd think sitting at a desk would be physically relaxing, or at least neutral, especially since I bought one of those expensive ergonomic chairs last year to make sure my posture was right. But no, even when I'm just sitting at my computer looking at data, I'm completely tense. It's like a coiled spring feeling. And it doesn't even stop when I log off for the day. Even after dinner, when I'm just trying to relax in the living room, maybe watch a little television or read a book on the couch, I can't just sink into the cushions and let go. I'm still wound up tight, just bracing myself. It's just so frustrating to feel this way all the time when I'm just trying to go about my normal daily routine, you know?

Susan, can you tell me if this feeling of being wound up started suddenly, or has it been building up over time? And can you think of any particular event or change in your life that might have triggered it?

Well, let me think... it definitely wasn't like a light switch just flipped on overnight. It was more of a gradual thing, sort of creeping up on me, building and building until one day I realized that I couldn't remember the last time my shoulders weren't practically up by my ears. If I really look back at the calendar and try to trace it to the source, I'd say this has been going on for about thirteen months now. 

And as for a trigger, yes, I actually can pinpoint exactly what was happening in my life around then. It was right when my sister—she lives down in Arecibo—started needing a whole lot more help from the family. It's just... well, it's incredibly hard being so far away, you know? Arecibo is a beautiful place, but when a family member suddenly needs you and you're thousands of miles away stuck at a desk looking at database architecture... it's just a lot to carry. 

We've all had to pitch in, of course, coordinating things and making sure she has what she needs, but because of my background, I'm sort of the designated organizer for the family. So I'm the one managing the logistics, figuring out who is doing what, checking in, and it created this constant hum of responsibility in the back of my mind. So, about thirteen months ago, when her situation changed and we really had to step up our involvement, that's exactly when this whole coiled-spring feeling really took root. I was managing my day-to-day life just fine before that, but once the family dynamics shifted and she needed us so much more, it's like my body just decided we always have to be on high alert now, just in case the phone rings. Even when I tell myself she's fine for the evening and there's nothing more I can do from here, I just can't seem to turn off that feeling of bracing for the next update.

Susan, in addition to feeling physically tense, have you noticed any other changes, like restlessness, trouble relaxing, trouble concentrating, irritability, trouble sleeping, or feeling fatigued more easily?

Well, gosh, since you mention it, sleep has definitely become a whole production lately. It’s not that I can’t fall asleep—usually, I’m so exhausted by the time I finally turn off the bedside lamp and stop scrolling through my phone, trying to make sure I haven't missed a text from my brother about who's taking my sister to her physical therapy... usually, I do manage to drift off. But staying asleep? That's the real trick, isn't it? 

Most nights, almost like clockwork, I’ll wake up right around three or four in the morning. And my brain just immediately turns on, like someone flipped a switch. I'll be lying there in the dark, staring at the ceiling, and suddenly I'm running through my sister’s next doctor's appointment, wondering if her insurance paperwork went through correctly, or if my brother remembered to ask the specialist about that new medication. And if it's not her, it's work. I'll start worrying about some server migration issue or a database query that was running slow before I logged off. I try all those tricks—deep breathing, counting backwards, trying to think of a relaxing beach—but my mind is just racing. 

And the worst part is, even on the nights where I do manage to string together enough hours, or when I finally fall back asleep just before my alarm goes off, I never actually feel refreshed. I start the morning feeling like I never really rested at all. It's like my body was working the night shift while I was supposedly sleeping. I drag myself out of bed, make my coffee, and I'm already exhausted before I even sit down at my desk to start my day. It's just a vicious cycle, really, because then I'm tired all day, which makes the tense feeling worse, and then I can't sleep well again the next night. It’s just... it’s a lot.
Susan, do you find yourself worrying excessively about a variety of things, like your job, family responsibilities, or other everyday issues, even when there isn't a clear reason for concern?

Oh, absolutely. Yes, I mean, that's really the heart of it, isn't it? It's just constant. It's like my brain is a television that's stuck flipping through channels, and every single channel is a different thing to worry about. I can't just settle on one thing, and I certainly can't just turn the television off. 

My mind just keeps going and going from one concern to another. Obviously, there's my sister down in Arecibo, which we talked about, and that's a big one. But it doesn't stop there. I'll be sitting at my desk, and suddenly I'm agonizing over whether I missed some tiny detail in a database migration at the office, even though I've checked the logs three times. Or... or I'll look at the clock and see it's raining outside, and immediately I'm terrified about my husband driving home from work in the slick conditions. I'll start imagining him hydroplaning on the interstate, and my chest just gets so tight until I hear his key in the door. 

And then there's the church commitments—I help organize the annual bake sale, which sounds so trivial, I know, but I'll lay awake worrying that we won't have enough volunteers or that the flyers didn't get printed right. And the bills! We're perfectly fine financially, both of us have good jobs, but I still find myself opening the banking app five times a day, just convinced that I forgot to pay the electric bill or that some massive unexpected expense is going to wipe out our savings. 

It's exhausting, doctor, because I find myself constantly preparing for problems that haven't even happened yet. It's like I'm playing out these disaster scenarios in my head, over and over, trying to figure out how I'll handle them if they do happen. And intellectually, I know there's no clear reason for most of this concern. I know my husband is a safe driver. I know the database is fine. I know the electric bill is on auto-pay. But my brain just won't accept that. It just keeps searching for the next thing that could possibly go wrong, and then fixating on it until I'm just tied up in knots over something that hasn't even occurred.
